claim: The study generated a single-nucleus atlas of the human hippocampus across neonatal, adult, aging, and injury states.
source: Based on our generated single-nucleus atlas of the human hippocampus across neonatal, adult, aging, and injury, we dissected the molecular heterogeneity and transcriptional dynamics of human hippocampal NSCs under different contexts.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that the authors generated a single-nucleus atlas across different ages and injury states.

claim: The study identified new specific neurogenic lineage markers that overcome the lack of specificity found in some well-known markers.
source: We further identified new specific neurogenic lineage markers that overcome the lack of specificity found in some well-known markers.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding as a result of the study.

claim: A subset of NSCs exhibit quiescent properties after birth.
source: Based on developmental trajectory and molecular signatures, we found that a subset of NSCs exhibit quiescent properties after birth, and most NSCs become deep quiescence during aging.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on developmental trajectory and molecular signatures.

claim: Most NSCs become deep quiescence during aging.
source: Based on developmental trajectory and molecular signatures, we found that a subset of NSCs exhibit quiescent properties after birth, and most NSCs become deep quiescence during aging.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on developmental trajectory and molecular signatures.

claim: Certain deep quiescent NSCs are reactivated following stroke injury.
source: Furthermore, certain deep quiescent NSCs are reactivated following stroke injury.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding.

claim: The dentate gyrus is part of the hippocampus and one of the main neurogenic niches.
source: The dentate gyrus (DG), a part of the hippocampus and one of the main neurogenic niches, sustains neurogenesis through the activity of resident neural stem cells (NSCs) (Berg et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Adult neurogenesis in rodents is well studied.
source: Although adult neurogenesis in rodents (Hochgerner et al., 2018; Dulken et al., 2017) is well studied, and age-related neurogenesis decline is conserved across species, whether hippocampal neurogenesis persists in the adult human brain has been debated over the years.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this with citations to support the claim.

claim: Age-related neurogenesis decline is conserved across species.
source: Although adult neurogenesis in rodents (Hochgerner et al., 2018; Dulken et al., 2017) is well studied, and age-related neurogenesis decline is conserved across species, whether hippocampal neurogenesis persists in the adult human brain has been debated over the years.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this as established knowledge.

claim: Whether hippocampal neurogenesis persists in the adult human brain has been debated over the years.
source: Although adult neurogenesis in rodents (Hochgerner et al., 2018; Dulken et al., 2017) is well studied, and age-related neurogenesis decline is conserved across species, whether hippocampal neurogenesis persists in the adult human brain has been debated over the years.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this as an ongoing debate in the field.

claim: Some studies found no evidence of neurogenesis in humans after adolescence based on marker immunostaining.
source: Based on marker immunostaining, a few studies found no evidence of neurogenesis in human after adolescence (Cipriani et al., 2018; Sorrells et al., 2018; Franjic et al., 2022), while others detected that human neurogenesis persists in adulthood but declines during aging (Boldrini et al., 2018; Moreno-Jiménez et al., 2019; Tobin et al., 2019; Terreros-Roncal et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this with citations to support the claim.

claim: Some studies detected that human neurogenesis persists in adulthood but declines during aging.
source: Based on marker immunostaining, a few studies found no evidence of neurogenesis in human after adolescence (Cipriani et al., 2018; Sorrells et al., 2018; Franjic et al., 2022), while others detected that human neurogenesis persists in adulthood but declines during aging (Boldrini et al., 2018; Moreno-Jiménez et al., 2019; Tobin et al., 2019; Terreros-Roncal et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this with citations to support the claim.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq can help resolve the ongoing debate about adult human neurogenesis.
source: It is expected that single-cell RNA-seq will help resolve the ongoing debate, as this technology is capable of bypassing the biases associated with traditional methods of immunostaining and quantification.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this expectation based on the capabilities of the technology.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq is capable of bypassing the biases associated with traditional methods of immunostaining and quantification.
source: It is expected that single-cell RNA-seq will help resolve the ongoing debate, as this technology is capable of bypassing the biases associated with traditional methods of immunostaining and quantification.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this as a capability of the technology.

claim: Single-cell analysis approaches can help identify novel cell markers and resolve the dynamics of transcriptional signatures during neurogenesis under different conditions.
source: Single-cell analysis approaches can also help identify novel cell markers and resolve the dynamics of transcriptional signatures during neurogenesis under different conditions.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this as a capability of single-cell analysis.

claim: One study failed to detect evidence of adult neurogenic trajectories in human hippocampal tissues using snRNA-seq.
source: Although one study failed to detect evidence of adult neurogenic trajectories in human hippocampal tissues (Franjic et al., 2022), the other two reported the presence of molecular programs consistent with the capacity for the adult human DG to generate new granule cells (GCs) (Zhou et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Two studies reported the presence of molecular programs consistent with the capacity for the adult human DG to generate new granule cells using snRNA-seq.
source: Although one study failed to detect evidence of adult neurogenic trajectories in human hippocampal tissues (Franjic et al., 2022), the other two reported the presence of molecular programs consistent with the capacity for the adult human DG to generate new granule cells (GCs) (Zhou et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this with citations to support the claim.

claim: Mouse NSCs gradually acquire quiescent properties and transform into quiescent NSCs with age.
source: Particularly, while actively proliferating in early development, mouse NSCs gradually acquire quiescent properties and transform into quiescent NSCs (qNSCs) with age.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this about mouse NSCs.

claim: Neurogenesis declines in the mouse aging hippocampus as a consequence of NSC loss and dormancy.
source: Although neurogenesis declines in the mouse aging hippocampus as a consequence of NSC loss and dormancy, qNSCs can be reactivated into active NSCs (aNSCs) that give rise to GCs which integrate into existing neural circuits (Encinas et al., 2011; Obernier and Alvarez-Buylla, 2019).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this with citations to support the claim.

claim: Quiescent NSCs can be reactivated into active NSCs that give rise to GCs which integrate into existing neural circuits in mice.
source: Although neurogenesis declines in the mouse aging hippocampus as a consequence of NSC loss and dormancy, qNSCs can be reactivated into active NSCs (aNSCs) that give rise to GCs which integrate into existing neural circuits (Encinas et al., 2011; Obernier and Alvarez-Buylla, 2019).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this with citations to support the claim.

claim: Ischemic insult in the adult mouse brain has been reported to evoke qNSC to transition into an active state.
source: Specifically, ischemic insult in the adult mouse brain has been reported to evoke qNSC to transition into an active state. However, whether these similar mechanisms occur in the human hippocampus is unknown (Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Whether similar mechanisms of qNSC reactivation occur in the human hippocampus is unknown.
source: Specifically, ischemic insult in the adult mouse brain has been reported to evoke qNSC to transition into an active state. However, whether these similar mechanisms occur in the human hippocampus is unknown (Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this as an unknown question.

claim: The study collected 10 donated post-mortem hippocampal tissues.
source: To generate a comprehensive cell atlas of neurogenic lineages in the human hippocampus, we collected 10 donated post-mortem hippocampal tissues.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this as part of the methodology.

claim: The study dissociated the anterior-mid hippocampus and performed 10x Genomics snRNA-seq.
source: We then dissociated the anterior-mid hippocampus (which has an obvious DG structure) and performed 10x Genomics snRNA-seq.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this as part of the methodology.

claim: The study performed immunostaining for the counterpart side of each hippocampus sample.
source: We also performed immunostaining for the counterpart side of each hippocampus sample (Figure 1A).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this as part of the methodology.

claim: The 10 individual samples were divided into four groups according to age and brain health: neonatal, adult, aging, and stroke-induced injury groups.
source: The 10 individual samples, divided into four groups according to age and brain health, included neonatal (day 4 after birth, D4, n=1), adult (31, 32 years of age, n=2), aging (from 50 to 68 years of age, n=6), and stroke-induced injury (48 years of age, n=1) groups (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this categorization.

claim: The study sequenced 99,635 single nuclei of which 92,966 nuclei were successfully retained after quality control and filtration.
source: In total, we sequenced 99,635 single nuclei of which 92,966 nuclei were successfully retained after quality control and filtration.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this data.

claim: A median of 3001 genes per nucleus was analyzed after quality control.
source: After the removal of cell debris, cell aggregates, and cells with more than 20% of mitochondrial genes transcripts, we analyzed a median of 3001 genes per nucleus. (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this data with reference to a figure.

claim: Human hippocampal cells were categorized into 16 main populations based on classical markers and differentially expressed genes.
source: To generate an overview of hippocampal cell types, we pooled single cells from all samples and categorized human hippocampal cells based on classical markers and differentially expressed genes (DEGs) into 16 main populations by Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this categorization with reference to figures.

claim: The 16 main populations include astrocyte1, astrocytes2/quiescent neural stem cell, pNSC, aNSC, NB, GC, GABA-IN, pyramidal neuron, oligodendrocyte progenitor, oligodendrocyte, microglia, endothelial cell, pericyte, Relin-expressing Cajal-Retzius cell, and two unidentified cell types.
source: These included astrocyte1 (AS1), astrocytes2/quiescent neural stem cell (AS2/qNSC), pNSC, aNSC, NB, GC, GABA-IN, pyramidal neuron (PN), oligodendrocyte progenitor (OPC), oligodendrocyte (OLG), microglia (MG), endothelial cell (EC), pericyte (Per), Relin-expressing Cajal-Retzius cell (CR), and two unidentified cell types (UN1, UN2).
evidence: The results section explicitly lists these populations.

claim: Some GCs were lost in the injured hippocampus according to cell percentages.
source: Although some GCs were lost in the injured hippocampus according to cell percentages, we found that pNSC and aNSC cell numbers decreased markedly with aging but were recovered in the stroke-injured hippocampus (Figure 1E).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: pNSC and aNSC cell numbers decreased markedly with aging but were recovered in the stroke-injured hippocampus.
source: Although some GCs were lost in the injured hippocampus according to cell percentages, we found that pNSC and aNSC cell numbers decreased markedly with aging but were recovered in the stroke-injured hippocampus (Figure 1E).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The average number of detected genes in each cell type is similar across different groups.
source: The average number of detected genes in each cell type is similar across different groups, thereby ruling out the possibility that the enrichment of stem cell genes is an artifact of increased global gene expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Cell compositions and proportions varied substantially in neonatal, adult, aging, and injured human hippocampus.
source: Overall, cell compositions and proportions varied substantially in neonatal, adult, aging, and injured human hippocampus (Figure 1E).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Human AS2/qNSCs and pNSCs aligned more strongly with astrocytes and radial glia-like cells from other species.
source: For example, human AS2/qNSCs and pNSCs aligned more strongly with astrocytes and radial glia-like cells (RGLs) from other species, and expressed classical RGL genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Human aNSCs and NBs clustered together with other species' neural intermediate progenitor cells and NBs.
source: Meanwhile, human aNSCs and NBs clustered together with other species' neural intermediate progenitor cells (nIPCs) and NBs, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Neurogenic lineage markers identified in other species were also highly expressed in corresponding populations in the study's data.
source: In addition, neurogenic lineage markers identified in other species were also highly expressed in corresponding populations in our data (Figure 2B).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The AS2/qNSC population from neonatal sample was subclustered into three clusters: astrocyte2, qNSC1, and qNSC2.
source: To this end, we performed further subclustering of the AS2/qNSC population by using Seurat (FindAllMarker) analysis (Figure 2C and D). According to the DEGs and the feature gene expression, three subclusters were identified and annotated as AS2, qNSC1, and qNSC2 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: The AS2 cluster obtained higher astrocyte score than qNSC1 and qNSC2.
source: Although the RGL gene set hardly distinguishes qNSCs from astrocytes (Figure 2E), analysis of astrocyte feature genes (Zamanian et al., 2012; Liddelow et al., 2017; Clarke et al., 2018; Hochgerner et al., 2018; Zhong et al., 2020; Franjic et al., 2022) revealed that the AS2 cluster obtained higher astrocyte score than qNSC1 and qNSC2 (Figure 2F).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures and citations.

claim: Classical astrocyte markers such as S100B and GFAP were highly expressed in the AS2 cluster.
source: The classical astrocyte markers such as S100B and GFAP were highly expressed in the AS2 cluster (Figure 2G).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The qNSC1 cluster was characterized by the preferred expression of quiescence NSC gene HOPX.
source: The qNSC1 cluster was characterized by the preferred expression of quiescence NSC gene HOPX.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The qNSC2 cluster behaved less quiescent than qNSC1 since they highly expressed LPAR1 and neurogenic genes.
source: Compared with the qNSC1 cluster, the qNSC2 cluster behaved less quiescent since they highly expressed LPAR1, neurogenic genes (e.g. STMN1, PROX1, SIRT2, and ST18), showing the initial potential of lineage development (Figure 2D and G).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: pNSCs lowly expressed ALDH1L1 and GFAP, but highly expressed stem cell genes HOPX, VIM, SOX2, SOX4, and CCND2.
source: Compared with astrocyte and qNSCs, pNSCs lowly expressed ALDH1L1 and GFAP, but highly expressed stem cell genes HOPX, VIM, SOX2, SOX4, and CCND2 (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: Gene ontology terms of the top 1000 genes in pNSCs included stem cell differentiation, Wnt signaling, neurogenesis, Notch signaling, and hippo signaling.
source: Consistent with their identities, gene ontology (GO) terms of the top 1000 genes in pNSCs included stem cell differentiation, Wnt signaling, neurogenesis, Notch signaling, and hippo signaling, indicating that they maintain critical properties of RGLs (Figure 2H).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: aNSCs highly expressed stem cell and proliferation markers, such as SOX2, SOX4, SOX11, and CCND2.
source: Different from pNSCs, the identified aNSCs highly expressed stem cell and proliferation markers, such as SOX2, SOX4, SOX11, and CCND2 (Figure 1C and D) and were enriched for GO terms associated with the onset of neuronal fate, such as neuron differentiation, neuron projection morphogenesis, axonogenesis, and synapse organization (Figure 2I).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: aNSCs were enriched for GO terms associated with the onset of neuronal fate, such as neuron differentiation, neuron projection morphogenesis, axonogenesis, and synapse organization.
source: Different from pNSCs, the identified aNSCs highly expressed stem cell and proliferation markers, such as SOX2, SOX4, SOX11, and CCND2 (Figure 1C and D) and were enriched for GO terms associated with the onset of neuronal fate, such as neuron differentiation, neuron projection morphogenesis, axonogenesis, and synapse organization (Figure 2I).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: NBs highly expressed CCND2, SOX4, STMN2, SOX11, PROX1, and NEUROD2, and started to express several GC markers, such as SYT1 and SV2B.
source: Different from NSCs, NBs highly expressed CCND2, SOX4, STMN2, SOX11, PROX1, and NEUROD2, and started to express several GC markers, such as SYT1 and SV2B (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: qNSC1 and qNSC2 were mainly in the non-cycling G0/G1 phase whereas aNSCs were mainly in the S/G2/M phase of active mitosis.
source: As expected, qNSC1 and qNSC2 were mainly in the non-cycling G0/G1 phase whereas aNSCs were mainly in the S/G2/M phase of active mitosis, confirming their quiescent and active cell states, respectively (Figure 2J).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: LRRC3B, RHOJ, SLC4A4, and GLI3 were specifically expressed in qNSC1 and qNSC2.
source: The combined results from scHPF and FindAllMarkers data showed that LRRC3B, RHOJ, SLC4A4, GLI3 were specifically expressed in qNSC1 and qNSC2, CHI3L1, and EGFR could be regarded as pNSC marker genes, and NRGN, NRN1, and HECW1 as NB marker genes at the transcriptional level (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: CHI3L1 and EGFR could be regarded as pNSC marker genes.
source: The combined results from scHPF and FindAllMarkers data showed that LRRC3B, RHOJ, SLC4A4, GLI3 were specifically expressed in qNSC1 and qNSC2, CHI3L1, and EGFR could be regarded as pNSC marker genes, and NRGN, NRN1, and HECW1 as NB marker genes at the transcriptional level (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: NRGN, NRN1, and HECW1 could be regarded as NB marker genes at the transcriptional level.
source: The combined results from scHPF and FindAllMarkers data showed that LRRC3B, RHOJ, SLC4A4, GLI3 were specifically expressed in qNSC1 and qNSC2, CHI3L1, and EGFR could be regarded as pNSC marker genes, and NRGN, NRN1, and HECW1 as NB marker genes at the transcriptional level (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: EGFR was specific for pNSCs, while CHI3L1 was also expressed by astrocytes.
source: Feature plots revealed that EGFR was specific for pNSCs, while CHI3L1 was also expressed by astrocytes. NRGN and NRN1 but not HECW1 were specific for NBs (Figure 3C).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: NRGN and NRN1 but not HECW1 were specific for NBs.
source: Feature plots revealed that EGFR was specific for pNSCs, while CHI3L1 was also expressed by astrocytes. NRGN and NRN1 but not HECW1 were specific for NBs (Figure 3C).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Several genes enriched in NBs, such as HECW1, STMN2, NSG2, SNAP25, and BASP1, were also widely distributed in GABA-INs.
source: Notably, several genes enriched in NBs, such as HECW1, STMN2, NSG2, SNAP25, and BASP1 (Figure 3C), were also widely distributed in GABA-INs that were validated by high expression of known GABA-IN marker genes, such as DLX1, GABRG3, CCK, SLC6A11, SLC6A1, GAD1, GAD2, CNR1, GRM1, RELN, and VIP (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: Previously reported genes that are regarded as the markers of NB/im-GCs, such as DCX, PROX1, and CALB2, were also enriched in neonatal GABA-INs.
source: Indeed, both the previously reported genes that are regarded as the markers of NB/im-GCs, such as DCX, PROX1, and CALB2 (Zhou et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022), and here identified genes (HECW1, STMN2, NSG2, SNAP25, and BASP1) were also enriched in neonatal GABA-INs (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures and citations.

claim: SST-positive interneurons are capable of being stained by the traditional NB marker DCX in primates.
source: To confirm the protein expression of DCX in interneurons, we conducted co-immunostainings of DCX and a typical interneuron marker (SST). Our results demonstrate that SST-positive interneurons are indeed capable of being stained by the traditional NB marker DCX in primates (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A—C).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: Identification of newborn neurons using NB/im-GC genes requires the exclusion of the interneuron contamination.
source: These results suggest that identification of newborn neurons using NB/im-GC genes requires the exclusion of the interneuron contamination, as reported by a recent study (Franjic et al., 2022).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this conclusion with a citation.

claim: Several representative NB/im-GC-specific genes were identified, such as CALM3, TTC9B, NRGN, FXYD7, NRN1, GNG3, TCEAL5, TMSB10, and NEUROD2.
source: We identified several representative NB/im-GC-specific genes, such as CALM3, TTC9B, NRGN, FXYD7, NRN1, GNG3, TCEAL5, TMSB10, and NEUROD2 (Figure 3F) and confirmed their specificity in adult and aging samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: pNSCs give two developmental directions: one is entering quiescence or generating AS2, and the other is generating aNSCs.
source: We used RNA velocity to investigate the developmental potentials of NSCs in the neonatal human hippocampus (Figure 4A). We observed that pNSCs give two developmental directions: one is entering quiescence or generating AS2, and the other is generating aNSCs.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: pNSCs were followed by aNSCs and NBs, and gave rise to two types of neurons (N1 and N2), indicative of ongoing neurogenesis.
source: According to the developmental trajectory, pNSCs were followed by aNSCs and NBs, and gave rise to two types of neurons (N1 and N2), indicative of ongoing neurogenesis (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: HOPX+NES+ RGLs and NES+Ki67+ active NSCs with long apical processes were detected in postnatal day 4 hippocampal dentate gyrus.
source: To validate the RNA-seq results, we performed immunostaining in the DG of D4 neonatal hippocampus. In the granule cell layer (GCL) and hilus, we detected HOPX+NES+ RGLs and Ki67+NES+ proliferating NSCs (Figure 4E), consistent with previously reported NSC immunostaining in human hippocampus (Sorrells et al., 2018).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: PSA-NCAM+ NBs located in the GCL as clusters in postnatal day 4 hippocampus.
source: We also found that PSA-NCAM+ NBs located in the GCL as clusters (Figure 4E).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Both pNSCs (RGLs) and aNSCs maintain their proliferative status and can generate new GCs in the neonatal human hippocampus.
source: These results confirm that both pNSCs (RGLs) and aNSCs maintain their proliferative status and can generate new GCs in the neonatal human hippocampus.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this conclusion based on the data.

claim: The ratios of qNSC1 and qNSC2 increased significantly with age, particularly the deep quiescent stem cell qNSC1.
source: When we quantified the cell numbers of different types of NSCs and their progeny across neonatal (postnatal day 4), adult (the mean of 31y, 32y), and aging (the mean of 50y, 56y, 60y, 64y-1, 64y-2, 68y) groups, we noted that the ratios of qNSC1 and qNSC2 increased significantly with age, particularly the deep quiescent stem cell qNSC1.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: pNSC and aNSC populations sharply declined from neonatal to adult and aging stages.
source: Conversely, pNSC and aNSC populations sharply declined from neonatal to adult and aging stages.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The numbers of NBs were comparable in the neonatal and adult brain, but they were markedly reduced in the aging hippocampus.
source: Meanwhile, the numbers of NBs were comparable in the neonatal and adult brain, but they were markedly reduced in the aging hippocampus (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: Immature neurons in primates are retained for a longer period and possess the potential to further develop into mature neurons compared to rodents.
source: The abundance of NBs in the adult brain suggest that compared to rodents, immature neurons in primates are indeed retained for a longer period and possess the potential to further develop into mature neurons (Kohler et al., 2011).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this interpretation with a citation.

claim: pNSCs and aNSCs are present in the neonatal hippocampus, but their numbers significantly decrease with age.
source: These results together showed that pNSCs and aNSCs are present in the neonatal hippocampus, but their numbers significantly decrease with age.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: Human neurogenesis experiences a rapid decline after birth.
source: This suggests that human neurogenesis experiences a rapid decline after birth.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: NBs have a longer maturation period until adulthood in humans.
source: In contrast, NBs have a longer maturation period until adulthood, which is consistent with previous studies (Ayhan et al., 2021; Franjic et al., 2022; Ngwenya et al., 2015; Seki, 2020).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with citations.

claim: Astrocyte and quiescence genes (LRRC3B, RHOJ, SLC4A4) were significantly up-regulated with increasing age.
source: We have observed a significant up-regulation of astrocyte and quiescence genes (LRRC3B, RHOJ, SLC4A4) with increasing age, as well as a marked down-regulation of pNSC genes (HOPX, SOX2, NES, VIM, and CHI3L1), aNSC genes (ASCL1, EOMES, and MKI67), and NB genes (STMN2, DCX) upon aging (Figure 5C).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: pNSC genes (HOPX, SOX2, NES, VIM, and CHI3L1), aNSC genes (ASCL1, EOMES, and MKI67), and NB genes (STMN2, DCX) were markedly down-regulated upon aging.
source: We have observed a significant up-regulation of astrocyte and quiescence genes (LRRC3B, RHOJ, SLC4A4) with increasing age, as well as a marked down-regulation of pNSC genes (HOPX, SOX2, NES, VIM, and CHI3L1), aNSC genes (ASCL1, EOMES, and MKI67), and NB genes (STMN2, DCX) upon aging (Figure 5C).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: NSC markers HOPX, VIM, NES, and CHI3L1, which were widely expressed in the neonatal D4 DG, were almost lost in 32y, 50y, and 56y DG.
source: When we stained hippocampal tissue sections from neonatal D4, 32y, and 56y donors (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), we observed that NSC markers HOPX, VIM, NES, and CHI3L1, which were widely expressed in the neonatal D4 DG, were almost lost in 32y, 50y, and 56y DG.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: VIM+ and NES+ RGLs were only present around the GCL or in the hilus of the neonatal DG (D4).
source: VIM+ and NES+ RGLs were only present around the GCL or in the hilus of the neonatal DG (D4); whereas the NB marker PSA-NCAM was expressed in the D4 and 32y DG, but not in 50y and 56y hippocampus (Figure 5D).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The NB marker PSA-NCAM was expressed in the D4 and 32y DG, but not in 50y and 56y hippocampus.
source: VIM+ and NES+ RGLs were only present around the GCL or in the hilus of the neonatal DG (D4); whereas the NB marker PSA-NCAM was expressed in the D4 and 32y DG, but not in 50y and 56y hippocampus (Figure 5D).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Cell proliferation and growth inhibition genes (BRINP1, CABLES1, TENM2, CNTN1), and stem cell differentiation genes (RANBP3L, NDRG2) were up-regulated significantly in qNSC1 during aging.
source: We observed that cell proliferation and growth inhibition genes (BRINP1, CABLES1, TENM2, CNTN1), and stem cell differentiation genes (RANBP3L, NDRG2) were up-regulated significantly in qNSC1 during aging.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Oligodendrocyte genes (MBP, PLP1, MOBP) were highly expressed in aging qNSC2.
source: Besides CABLES1 and CNTN1, the oligodendrocyte genes (MBP, PLP1, MOBP) were also highly expressed in aging qNSC2 (Figure 5E).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Stem cell and regeneration genes (LPAR1, TNC, CASC15, SOX2, SOX4, HOPX, VIM) were down-regulated in qNSC1 and qNSC2 during aging.
source: In contrast, stem cell and regeneration genes (LPAR1, TNC, CASC15, SOX2, SOX4, HOPX, VIM) were down-regulated in qNSC1 and qNSC2 (Figure 5E).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Hippocampal NSCs undergo a transition into a state of deep quiescence and acquire glial properties during aging.

We detected a few NES+KI67+, NES+VIM+, and NES+CHI3L1+ aNSCs that had radial glia morphology with apical processes (Figure 6B), appearing similar to D4 NES+ RGLs (Figure 4E).
